opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting questions in our field right now, and honestly one I've thought about a lot, because my background is in physically based simulation, which is about as "traditional graphics" as it gets.

When Sora first came out, a lot of people asked me, "Is graphics dead? Why would you solve Navier–Stokes equations if a neural network can just generate a video of smoke?" My view is that video models have changed the role of graphics, but they haven't replaced it. They've shifted where the value lies.

Traditional graphics was always about two things. One is realism: making images that look right. The other is control: being able to say exactly where this object is, what this material is, how this camera moves, and getting the same result every time. Video models have made a huge leap on the first one. You can get visually stunning results without modeling anything explicitly. That's a real breakthrough, and I don't think we should be defensive about it.

But on the second axis, control, consistency, editability, and physical correctness, there's still a big gap. If you're a game developer, you can't ship a video. You need assets: meshes, textures, rigs, something an engine can run interactively at 60 frames per second, from any viewpoint, responding to the player. If you're an engineer simulating a car crash or a fluid in a pipe, "plausible-looking" isn't enough. You need the numbers to be right. Video models today don't really have an explicit 3D representation or conservation laws. Sometimes a glass of water spills and the water disappears, or a hand gains a sixth finger halfway through.

So I see the role of traditional graphics moving in a few directions. First, it becomes the structure underneath. Explicit 3D representations, physics, and rendering act as scaffolding that makes generative output controllable and consistent. Second, graphics pipelines are becoming data engines. Simulators and renderers produce training data with perfect ground truth, which is very hard to get from the real world. Third, the interface changes. Instead of an artist spending weeks modeling a character vertex by vertex, AI can produce a strong first draft in seconds, and graphics tools let people refine it. That's actually a big part of why I moved toward 3D generative AI myself. I felt the most impactful thing was to combine the two worlds rather than pick one.

Longer term, I think the boundary will get blurry. We'll see hybrid systems where neural networks handle the parts that are hard to model by hand, like appearance, fine detail, and messy real-world complexity, while classical methods handle the parts where we really know the math, like geometry, physics, and light transport. The people who understand both sides will be in a very good position.

So my short answer is that video models didn't kill computer graphics. They raised the bar on what "looking real" means for free, and pushed graphics researchers to focus on what really matters: control, interactivity, and correctness.

r001.rationale: The response says graphics can provide scaffolding and training data for generative systems, but does not credit it with helping enable Sora’s emergence.

r002.rationale: It predicts hybrid systems combining neural networks with classical graphics methods, not that learning will become the primary approach.

r003.rationale: It describes simulators as sources of training data, but does not predict that simulators will become part of learnable modules.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and honestly it's one I've thought about a great deal, because my whole background is in traditional graphics, physics simulation, differentiable programming, Taichi, all of that. So when Sora came out, my first reaction was a mix of excitement and, I'll be honest, a little bit of existential anxiety.

But the more I've looked at it, the more I think the right framing isn't "video models replace graphics." It's that they've changed what the graphics pipeline is for.

Think about what traditional graphics is really good at. It's explicit. You have geometry, you have materials, you have lights, you have a physics solver that tells you exactly where the fluid goes. Everything is controllable and everything is consistent. If I move the camera two inches to the left, I know exactly what I'll get. The cost is that building all of that is incredibly expensive. You need artists, you need technical directors, you need a whole simulation setup, and you still end up rendering something that looks "CG."

Video models flip that completely. They're implicit. You describe what you want and you get something that looks astonishingly real, with lighting and motion that would take a studio weeks to set up. But you lose the handles. You can't say "make the water splash exactly here, and keep the character's face identical across these three shots." The model has learned a kind of intuitive physics from watching a lot of video, but it's not a physics engine. It makes plausible mistakes, and in production, plausible mistakes are still mistakes.

So where I think things are going, and this is really what we've been building toward, is that the two become partners rather than competitors. Traditional graphics becomes the control layer. You use a simulator or a 3D scene to provide the structure, the camera path, the rough motion, the object layout, and then the generative model does what it's best at, which is filling in appearance and realism. Graphics gives you the "what" and "where," the video model gives you the "how it looks."

There's also a very practical angle. Simulation can generate enormous amounts of perfectly labeled training data, with ground truth physics, that the real world simply can't give you. So in a funny way, the same physics solvers people assumed would be obsolete are becoming the thing that makes the next generation of video models actually understand the world instead of just imitating it.

And the last shift, which I think people underestimate, is who gets to make things. Traditional graphics was a specialist's tool. It took me years to get decent at it. Video models put a meaningful chunk of that capability in front of anyone with a sentence to type. That doesn't eliminate the expert, but it changes the expert's job from pushing every pixel to directing, constraining, and correcting. Which, if you ask me, is a much more interesting job anyway.

r001.rationale: The response describes traditional graphics and simulation as partners for future video models, but does not say they helped enable Sora’s emergence.

r002.rationale: It predicts a partnership between graphics and generative models, not that learning will become the primary approach in computer graphics.

r003.rationale: It presents simulators as sources of structure and training data, but does not predict that they will become learnable modules.

astra-6.text:
I think models like Sora change how we think about generating visual content. In traditional computer graphics, we explicitly describe a scene—its geometry, materials, lighting, and motion—and then render it. With a video model, you can describe what you want in words and get something visually compelling. That makes it much easier to explore ideas without building every component first.

But producing a convincing video and building a controllable world are different capabilities. If you’re making a game, for example, you need the world to respond to a player’s actions. You need objects to behave consistently, and you need to be able to change one thing without unexpectedly changing everything else. Traditional graphics gives you explicit ways to control those things.

So I see an opportunity to combine the two. Generative models can make content creation easier, while graphics and simulation can provide structure and control. The interesting question is how much we should generate directly and where an explicit representation of the world is still useful.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts traditional graphics with video models and proposes combining them, but does not credit traditional graphics with enabling Sora’s emergence.

r002.rationale: It describes generative models as making content creation easier, but does not predict that learning will become the primary approach in computer graphics.

r003.rationale: It mentions graphics and simulation providing structure and control, but does not say simulators will become learnable modules.

sol-6.1.text:
I think models like Sora change how we create visual content, but they don’t make traditional computer graphics obsolete. They give us a very different way to generate video: instead of explicitly building every object, material, and animation, you can describe what you want and get something visually compelling.

But looking plausible and being controllable are different things. If you’re making a film or designing a product, you may need the same object to behave consistently across shots, a camera to follow an exact path, or a simulation to obey particular physical constraints. Traditional graphics gives you explicit representations and tools to control those things.

So I see a lot of opportunity in combining the two. Video models can help with generation and exploration, while geometry, rendering, and simulation provide structure and control. The interesting question is how to make those pieces work together so that creating something becomes much easier, without losing the ability to specify exactly what you want.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts video models with traditional graphics and suggests combining them, but does not say traditional computer graphics helped enable Sora.

r002.rationale: It describes video models as a different generation method but does not predict that learning will become the primary approach in computer graphics.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulation as a source of structure and control, but does not predict simulators will become learnable modules.
